item.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
item.description:
Members of 350.org attend a demonstration calling for an electrification target based on renewable energy, not fossil fuels at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Members of 350.org attend a demonstration calling for an electrification target based on renewable energy, not fossil fuels at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters
China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.
But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

item.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
item.description:
Donald Trump takes questions from reporters in the White House press briefing room on Friday. Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Donald Trump takes questions from reporters in the White House press briefing room on Friday. Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty Images
Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi
Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.
In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.
“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
“We want them to build it here.”

item.title: Friend zone: rejected by US voters, Trump enjoys autocrats’ warm embrace
item.description:
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters
Friend zone: rejected by US voters, Trump enjoys autocrats’ warm embrace
The US president rated his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin as 12 out of 10 but China and Russia had the most to celebrate
He got by with a little help from his friends. Rebuked by millions of voters in a still resilient democracy, Donald Trump travelled to Asia this week and found comfort in the company of autocrats who still flatter him.
The US president, reduced to lame-duck status at home by a humiliating midterm election defeat, returned to the global stage in a meeting with two strongmen in Shenzhen, China, that critics described as a new low for America’s claim to moral authority.
“Who is he?” Trump asked rhetorically, pointing as he walked towards the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin. “He’s my friend.” Separately he told the Chinese president, Xi Jinping: “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship.”Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
Read more
Trump, Xi and Putin convened at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, for the first-ever trilateral summit among the leaders of the US, China and Russia, the world’s three biggest nuclear powers. The official product of their 70-minute closed-door meeting was a four-point document titled the “Declaration Toward Peace” that made no mention of the wars in Iran or Ukraine.

item.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
item.description:

View image in fullscreen
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Jensen Huang (pictured) admitted to the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low on Thursday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images
California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.Nvidia approaches Arm boss Rene Haas in search for new CEO
Read more
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

item.title: Xi Jinping says a ‘full turnaround’ has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese
item.description:
After an intense diplomatic campaign, Anthony Albanese received a warm welcome from China’s president, Xi Jinping, on Friday. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP
View image in fullscreen
After an intense diplomatic campaign, Anthony Albanese received a warm welcome from China’s president, Xi Jinping, on Friday. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP
Xi Jinping says a ‘full turnaround’ has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese
Comments come after the leaders met on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China
Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast
Xi Jinping says a “full turnaround” has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese as the pair met in Shenzhen on Friday.
The two leaders held talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, as the federal government continues efforts to stabilise trade and security relations with Beijing after a rocky period under the former Coalition government.
Beijing launched a punishing round of trade tariffs after efforts by Australia to keep Chinese telecommunications firm Huawei from taking part in the rollout of 5G mobile services – and after calls from the Morrison government for a full international investigation in the origins of the Covid-19 pandemic.
About $20bn in tariffs were added to key Australian exports, including barley, wine, beef, lobsters, coal and timber.
But, after an intense diplomatic campaign and the lifting of many of the tariffs, the Australian leader received a warm welcome from Xi on Friday.
He welcomed Albanese at Kylin Villa, the sprawling complex where he hosted US president, Donald Trump, and Russian president, Vladimir Putin, a day earlier.
“China-Australia friendship is what the people want,” Xi said.

item.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
item.description:
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the trilateral talks in China. Photograph: White House Office/APAImages/Shutterstock
View image in fullscreen
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the trilateral talks in China. Photograph: White House Office/APAImages/Shutterstock
China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

item.title: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
item.description:
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.
